prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: دورات تدريبية معتمدة (language ar, right-to-left: column 1 is on the RIGHT).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "اسم الدورة" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 250px
  col 2: header "المدة" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 168px
  col 3: header "المدرب" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 105px
  col 4: header "الوصف" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 1420px
  col 5: header "الرسوم" · longest unbreakable word 43px · one-line width 70px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"A catalog of accredited training courses that readers scan to compare offerings and shortlist by course topic, duration, trainer, and fee; the description supports the choice after the course name is identified.","reading":"Right-to-left: the eye starts at the rightmost course-name column as the row anchor, then moves left through duration and trainer metadata, the descriptive text, and finally the fee at the far left; cross-row comparison is strongest on course name, duration, trainer, and fee.","groups":["col 1 (اسم الدورة) is the row anchor and identity column","col 2 (المدة) and col 3 (المدرب) are delivery metadata and scan together","col 4 (الوصف) is narrative detail, read after the shortlist","col 5 (الرسوم) is a separate commercial figure and should remain compact and intact"],"keep_intact":["course-name words, especially the 67px longest token","trainer names","fee figures","duration numbers and their unit words","header labels, especially المدرب and الرسوم"],"may_wrap":["الوصف extensively at word boundaries","course names at word boundaries when necessary","duration phrases such as \"5 أيام (25 ساعة)\" at spaces","trainer names into two lines if needed"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[210,110,110,220,69],"idea":"Balanced allocation: give the title and description comparable room while keeping duration, trainer, and fee compact enough for two-line metadata."},{"name":"B","widths":[170,90,100,290,69],"idea":"Description-led: sacrifice title and metadata width so the very long description wraps least, since it is the only column with 1420px of one-line text."},{"name":"C","widths":[271,94,95,190,69],"idea":"Title-led: keep course names essentially on one line and compress duration and trainer into narrow wrapped stacks, treating the description as secondary reading."}]}
